title: Decidability of subsequence constraints with regular domains
formal: For each fixed finite alphabet \(A\), consider the following decision problem. An input consists of a finite set \(X\) of variables, one regular expression \(r_x\) over \(A\) for every \(x\in X\), and a finite list \(C\) of constraints \(x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k\), where \(x,y_i\in X\) and \(k\ge0\). Does there exist, for every fixed \(A\), a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every such input and decides whether there is an assignment \(h:X\to A^*\) satisfying \[h(x)\in L(r_x)\quad(x\in X),\qquad h(x)\preceq h(y_1)\cdots h(y_k)\quad((x\preceq y_1\cdots y_k)\in C)?\] The same variable may occur repeatedly, and the directed dependencies between variables may contain arbitrary cycles.
why: This question isolates the effect of cyclic reuse of unknown strings in a small constraint language. Regular domains and ordered concatenation are basic operations in string analysis, while subsequence constraints model loss of letters. A resolution would identify whether these ingredients alone retain effective satisfiability testing, clarifying a boundary obscured by undecidability results for richer interfaces.
status_note: Source-open in the checked July 2024 problem statement and March 2024 primary paper. On 15 September 2026 a bounded later-work search found no matching resolution. Acyclic algorithms and richer-model undecidability do not settle this exact syntax; paper proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The published STACS paper gives an NEXPTIME decision bound for acyclic regular constraints even in its richer model. Its §6.2 leaves decidability open when regular constraints use only concatenation and arbitrary cycles are allowed; the undecidability constructions discussed there require operations absent here.
Automata Exchange records the exact question with one variable on each left side, a word of variables on each right side, and regular-expression domains.

The original problem page and the precise open passage in STACS 2024 were rechecked. A bounded search of subsequent work did not locate a resolution matching these constraints. This is a dated source-status report, not an independent proof that the question remains open.

sentences: Each variable denotes one finite word constrained to a specified regular language.
A relational constraint requires that word to occur as a scattered subsequence of a concatenation of other assigned words.
The question asks for total decidability over every fixed finite alphabet, allowing repeated variables and arbitrary dependency cycles.
Known algorithms for acyclic systems and undecidability results with shuffle or transducers concern different input classes.
A resolution would locate the decidability boundary of a basic language for relating incomplete and concatenated strings.

definitions: A word over \(A\) is a finite sequence of its letters; \(A^*\) contains the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Concatenation appends sequences in their given order. For words \(u=u_1\cdots u_m\) and \(v=v_1\cdots v_n\), \(u\preceq v\) means that there exist indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(u_j=v_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). Thus it is the scattered-subsequence relation, including \(\varepsilon\preceq v\). For \(k=0\), the right-hand side evaluates to \(\varepsilon\). Every occurrence of a variable receives the same assigned word. A regular expression is a finite syntax tree generated by letters of \(A\), \(\varnothing\), \(\varepsilon\), binary union, concatenation and Kleene star; its language is defined by these operations, with star allowing any finite number of repetitions, including zero. Variables may receive empty words exactly when their domain expressions permit them. The input explicitly lists the expression trees and variable occurrences, using binary integer indices and delimiters; no compressed strings, numeric length predicates or additional relation symbols occur. A dependency edge \(x\to y\) is present if \(y\) occurs on the right of a constraint whose left side is \(x\). No acyclicity promise is imposed. Up to renaming, the alphabet can be written \(A=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) for \(a\in\mathbb N\). The quantifier order is \(\forall a\,\exists M_a\,\forall I\): one finite machine for every instance over that fixed alphabet. This preserves the source's fixed-alphabet convention; it does not demand an effective construction of \(M_a\) from \(a\). Machines must terminate with the exact answer on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. No time or space bound is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified decidability statement or its negation. A positive result must provide total, correct decision procedures covering every finite system over every fixed finite alphabet with exactly the syntax above. A negative result must prove that for at least one fixed finite alphabet no such total computable decision procedure exists. Deciding only systems with acyclic dependencies, or proving undecidability after adding shuffle, transducers, concatenations on the left, or nonregular domain languages, does not settle this statement.

context_blocks.text: A domain expression describes the possible complete value of one variable. A constraint such as \(x\preceq yz\) asks that this value survive as a subsequence after the values of \(y\) and \(z\) are joined. The assignment is shared across the whole system, so different constraints cannot choose independent values for the same variable.

The left side is always one variable, whereas the right side may repeat and concatenate variables. This syntactic asymmetry matters: the card does not ask for arbitrary pairs of concatenated terms related by subsequence. The open question also permits dependencies that return to an earlier variable; results requiring acyclicity cover only part of this domain.

The STACS paper studies a broader language that can interleave strings by shuffle and transform them by finite-state transducers. Its acyclic regular fragment is decidable, while general cyclic fragments of that richer language are undecidable. Section 6.2 explicitly separates the present concatenation-only, transducer-free case as unresolved. Those neighboring theorems therefore do not justify retiring this card.

source_formulation.text: Decide whether a finite collection of scattered-subsequence constraints from a variable to a concatenation of variables has an assignment satisfying the given regular domains.
